lesson_title: The Two Moments of a Credit Sale
hook_text: A builder pays you R6 000 today for goods he took three weeks ago. How much did you earn today? Nothing.
clip_script: On 3 April, Hilltop Builders takes R6 000 of goods on credit. They cost the shop R4 000. Moment one: the goods go. The shop now has a debtor: Hilltop owes R6 000. Sales up R6 000. Stock down R4 000. Profit: R2 000, earned today, even though no money has arrived. On 20 April, Hilltop pays R6 000. Moment two: the money comes. Bank up R6 000. Debtors down R6 000. Owner's equity? Unchanged. Not one rand of new income. Why? Because the sale was already counted on 3 April. Count it again and you have invented a sale that never happened. A credit sale earns its profit the day the goods leave. The payment just swaps a promise for cash. Cash sale or credit sale, the profit is the same. Only the asset changes: bank, or debtors.
visual_style: A calendar flipping from 3 April to 20 April, a box of goods leaving a shop with a profit tag appearing, then a promise note turning into bank notes with a zero-profit stamp.
pacing: A hook question, two clearly separated moments, a firm rule at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and analyse four April transactions in the accounting equation.
